html:
The Mainframe Is Not Dead. But It Is Expensive.

A mid-size mutual carrier we worked with was running a COBOL-based policy admin system from the early 1990s. Their IT team had institutional knowledge locked in a handful of engineers who were, bluntly, approaching retirement. Every regulatory change in their state required a six-to-eight week development cycle just to push a rate update. Their straight-through processing (STP) rate for new term applications sat around 34%. They knew this was a problem. What surprised them was how much it was costing them to keep it a problem.

This is not some edge case. According to Celent’s 2024 Model Insurer report, more than 60% of North American life carriers still run policy administration on systems older than 20 years. Some of that is COBOL mainframe. Some is early-generation client-server. And a growing segment is a hybrid patchwork that, honestly, nobody fully understands anymore. The question heading into 2026 is not whether to modernize. It’s which path delivers measurable returns without capsizing the business during transition.

What the Benchmark Data Actually Shows

Before getting into architecture debates, let’s look at real numbers. The table below draws from Celent’s Model Insurer data and LIMRA’s 2023-2024 digital transformation benchmarking studies to compare legacy mainframe environments against cloud-native life insurance administration software platforms.

Metric COBOL/Mainframe Legacy Cloud-Native Modern Platform Source
Straight-Through Processing (STP) Rate 28-42% 72-91% Celent Model Insurer 2024
Time to Market for New Product 9-18 months 2-5 months LIMRA Digital Transformation 2023
IT Maintenance as % of Total IT Budget 65-78% 30-45% Celent Model Insurer 2024
Average Cost Per Policy (Annual Admin) $180-$310 $95-$160 LIMRA Digital Transformation 2023
Regulatory Change Implementation Time 6-14 weeks 1-3 weeks Celent Model Insurer 2024
API-Ready Integration Capability Limited (batch, MQ) Native REST/GraphQL Vendor documentation (Majesco, EXL, Sapiens)
Carrier Satisfaction Score (Ops Teams) 54/100 78/100 LIMRA Digital Transformation 2023

The STP gap is what tends to move actuaries and operations leaders most. Going from 34% to 85% STP on term applications translates directly to headcount savings, faster policy issuance, and fewer good-order rejection loops. LIMRA’s research shows carriers who hit STP rates above 80% report 23% lower per-application processing costs versus peers still relying on manual intervention cycles baked into legacy workflows. That gap compounds every year you delay.

Cloud-Native Platforms: Real Capabilities, Real Caveats

Vendors like Majesco, Sapiens ALIS, EXL LifePRO, and Equisoft have built modern life insurance software stacks running on AWS, Azure, or GCP with true multi-tenancy, configurable product engines, and API-first architectures. That last part matters enormously for carriers trying to connect to e-application platforms, underwriting decision engines like Underwriting Insight or RGA’s automated underwriting tools, and digital distribution partners.

The product configurability story is genuinely good on these platforms. A carrier launching a new indexed universal life (IUL) rider no longer needs a six-month development sprint. In most modern policy administration software environments, product managers work inside no-code or low-code product definition tools that push to a rules engine without touching application code. That is a real capability shift, not marketing language.

But here is where I would pump the brakes hard. The “lift and shift” failure mode is very real. We have seen carriers move data to a cloud-native platform, replicate every broken legacy process in the new environment, and then genuinely wonder why their STP rates did not improve. The platform does not fix bad workflow design. If your new business rules are a mess on the mainframe, they will be a mess in the cloud unless you do the painful process redesign work in parallel with the technology migration. Nobody wants to hear that. It is still true.

Data migration is also harder than most vendors will tell you during the sales process. Historical policy data in COBOL flat files is deeply denormalized. Field mappings, legacy product codes, and exception states accumulated over 20-plus years can take 12 to 18 months to clean, map, and validate. Budget for that honestly, not optimistically.

The Mainframe Case: Unfashionable But Not Irrational

There are situations where keeping the mainframe makes cold economic sense, at least near-term. A carrier with 2 million in-force policies, a small IT team, and no near-term product expansion ambitions may find that total cost of ownership (TCO) for a platform replacement exceeds operational savings within a 5-year horizon. That is not a technology failure. It’s math.

IBM Z-series mainframes running COBOL can process enormous transaction volumes with extremely high reliability. Batch processing overnight for billing, commissions, and dividend calculations on a system that has run without failure for 15 years is genuinely hard to argue against on raw stability grounds. Conversations about mainframe modernization solutions often underweight this reliability track record, because nobody in a conference session gets applause for saying “our old system works fine.”

The legitimate concern is what happens at the edges. Regulatory compliance agility is where legacy systems genuinely struggle. State insurance departments have accelerated their pace of regulatory change since 2020 – AG 49-A updates, new illustration regulation amendments, evolving LTCI rate approval requirements. Implementing those in a COBOL environment means finding a programmer who knows COBOL (an increasingly scarce and expensive skill) and then navigating a change management process that may require regression testing across thousands of product configurations. That is expensive. And it keeps getting more expensive every year you stay put.

The other quiet killer is the talent pipeline. The average age of a COBOL developer in the US is now over 50, according to Micro Focus (now OpenText) survey data. Succession planning for your core admin system codebase is a real risk factor that does not show up cleanly in a TCO spreadsheet but absolutely belongs in the conversation.

Insurance Policy Administration Systems: How to Actually Choose

This is where a lot of RFP processes go sideways. Carriers issue a 200-question RFI, get back 200 “yes” answers from every vendor, and then struggle to differentiate on anything meaningful. Here is a buyer’s checklist built around the dimensions that actually separate strong implementations from expensive disappointments.

Buyer’s Checklist for Life Carriers Selecting or Replacing Core Admin Systems

  • STP architecture review: Ask vendors to walk through exactly which decision points in the new business workflow are fully automated versus queued for manual review. Get their actual client benchmarks, not theoretical maximums. Reference clients with similar product mixes, meaning term, whole life, UL, and annuities, are the only ones that count here.
  • Regulatory update SLA: What is the contractual commitment for implementing a state-mandated regulatory change, and who bears the development cost? Some SaaS models include regulatory updates in the base fee. Others bill for every single change. Know which model you are buying before you sign anything.
  • Data migration methodology: Request a sample data migration playbook. If the vendor cannot produce one, walk away. Ask specifically how they handle orphaned records, legacy exception states, and historical claims data.
  • Integration layer depth: Does the platform support real-time API integration with your preferred underwriting, reinsurance, and distribution systems? Get a list of live integration partners, not “available connectors” that are really just roadmap items. Majesco, for instance, publishes an exchange marketplace. Check what is actually live.
  • Product configuration tool evaluation: Have your product actuary and a business analyst sit in a hands-on demo where they configure a simplified IUL product themselves. Not a scripted demo. An actual sandbox exercise. This surfaces usability gaps faster than any RFI question ever will.
  • TCO over 7 years: Model out licensing, implementation, data migration, training, ongoing configuration, and regulatory update costs over a 7-year window. Most carriers significantly underestimate years 3 through 5. Ask for references from clients who are at least 4 years post-go-live and talk to them without the vendor present.
  • Cloud tenancy model: Single-tenant vs. multi-tenant has real implications for data isolation, upgrade scheduling, and customization limits. Neither is universally better. Align this with your own data governance and compliance posture rather than letting the vendor steer you to whatever is cheapest for them to support.
  • Exit strategy: What does data portability look like if you switch vendors in 10 years? Vendors will not volunteer to answer this. Ask it anyway, and get something contractual.

One practical note on evaluating insurance policy administration systems: visit reference clients in person or on a video call, and do it without the vendor present. The stories carriers tell without a vendor in the room are dramatically different from the case studies on the vendor’s website. Every time.

What to Expect in 2026 and Beyond

The modernization wave is real and accelerating. LIMRA’s 2024 benchmarking data shows 41% of life carriers have either completed or are actively mid-implementation on a core admin platform replacement, up from 27% in 2021. That is a significant shift in a traditionally conservative industry.

A few specific trends are reshaping what “modern” even means for life insurance administration software in 2026. Embedded AI for underwriting decisioning is moving from experimental to production at carriers running modern platforms. Sapiens and Majesco both have AI-assisted underwriting modules that sit inside the policy admin workflow, not bolted on externally as an afterthought. Real-time reinsurance connectivity, particularly for automated facultative decisions on accelerated underwriting programs, is becoming a baseline expectation rather than a differentiator. And carriers are increasingly demanding composable architecture, meaning the ability to swap out individual modules like billing, document generation, or the agent portal without replacing the entire platform. That last one is going to separate serious vendors from the rest fairly quickly.

Carriers still on mainframe systems are not locked out of innovation entirely. Incremental mainframe modernization solutions like API wrappers, think Heirloom or Micro Focus COBOL modernization tooling, can expose legacy data and transactions to modern front-ends without a full rip-and-replace. This is a legitimate intermediate step for carriers who need 2 to 3 years to fund and plan a full migration. Just treat it as a bridge with a defined end date, not a permanent answer.

FAQ

How long does a full life insurance administration software replacement typically take?

For a mid-size carrier with 500,000 to 2 million in-force policies, realistic timelines run 18 to 36 months from contract signing to full production cutover. Smaller carriers with simpler product sets have done it in 12 to 18 months. Larger carriers with complex product portfolios and heavy customization needs have taken 4-plus years. The data migration and parallel-run testing phases almost always take longer than originally projected. Build in at least a 25% buffer on whatever estimate your systems integrator gives you, and do not let them talk you out of that buffer.

What is the typical total cost of ownership difference between mainframe and cloud-native policy administration software?

Celent’s research suggests that over a 10-year horizon, cloud-native platforms tend to run 30-45% lower in total IT cost for life carriers, once you account for hardware maintenance, COBOL talent costs, and the increasing frequency of regulatory change implementation work on legacy systems. That said, the migration itself is a significant upfront investment, typically $5 million to $25 million depending on carrier size and complexity, and some of that cost advantage takes 4 to 5 years to materialize. Model both scenarios honestly before committing.

Can a carrier modernize incrementally without replacing the entire core admin system?

Yes, and this is actually what a meaningful portion of the market is doing right now. API wrapping the mainframe to expose data to modern digital channels, migrating new product lines to a cloud platform while keeping legacy products on the mainframe, implementing a modern rules engine in front of the COBOL core, these are all viable intermediate strategies. The risk is complexity accumulation. Managing two parallel systems creates real operational overhead and integration debt that piles up quietly. It works best as a defined 3-to-5-year bridge with an actual end state in mind, not a permanent architecture you just stop thinking about.
